prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat-band systems

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B013 as a single-part prize with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. The chair asks which criterion should decide between B061 and B013, and I state mine explicitly: the prize is for a discovery or invention of great benefit, and where two candidates are both sound and confirmed, I give weight to whether nature was shown to contain something that was not anticipated to be reachable, and to whether the finding reorganised a field. Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene meets this on both counts. A parameter-free continuum model predicted flat bands at a specific twist angle, the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity there, and many independent groups have since reproduced these phases and extended them to other moire systems, where new states keep appearing. A single geometric parameter now tunes bandwidth and interaction strength in a controlled way, which is a conceptual change for the physics of correlated matter and not just a new material. On the chair's maturity question I regard the unresolved pairing mechanism as a matter of follow-on physics. What would be honoured is the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, both of which are secure, and the citation can be worded around them without any claim about mechanism. Eight years with broad reproduction is not early compared with other recent condensed-matter recognitions.
statement.case_against: The case against is real, and I weigh it more heavily than I did in round 1. First, attribution: Yuan Cao and Valla Fatemi, first authors of the 2018 experiments, and Dean, Young, Ashoori and the earlier theorists Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are outside the three-name set, and no principled rule removes all of the discomfort. Second, the field is still moving, so a later prize might be better informed about which of the correlated states are the lasting results. Third, B061 has a cleaner two-name credit, complete independent confirmation and a precisely defined result, and several colleagues whose judgement I trust in atomic physics (Lindroth, Kroll) say that the physics of the magic wavelength and the blackbody shift is sound. If the committee decides that cleanliness of claim and credit should decide, B061 is a defensible choice and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Lindroth rests B061 on atomic-structure physics she can judge directly (magic wavelength, blackbody shift), argues that the 2005 comb prize and 2012 single-system prize did not recognise the neutral-atom lattice clock, and asks that B061 and B013 be tested on the same criteria rather than by counting first places.
responses.response: I accept the substance. The magic-wavelength and blackbody-shift physics is as sound as she says, and her point that the comb prize enabled the clocks without recognising the lattice-clock concept answers the overlap worry I raised in round 1, which I now drop as a decisive objection. I do not accept that this makes B061 the stronger candidate. Using the criterion I state above, B013 reveals a new regime in which interactions and band structure are tunable together, while B061 takes an established measurement to a new level and its largest fundamental-physics payoff is still prospective. Her test is fair, and applying it to both, I still come out with B013 first and B061 as a close second. I would also like her to say whether she thinks the 10^-18 milestones can be assigned to Ye with Katori for the concept, or whether the group spread she lists would make her uncomfortable with a two-name credit.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock claim is exact, measured and not open to reinterpretation, whereas B013 would honour a platform whose central superconducting physics is not settled, and he would rather give a fully defensible prize.
responses.response: I agree that the clock claim is exact and settled, and I agree that it has the cleanest credit. Where I disagree is the inference from the unresolved pairing mechanism to a defect in the prize. The existence of the flat bands and of the correlated insulating and superconducting phases is established and does not hinge on any theory of pairing, so the citation I propose says nothing about mechanism. A settled claim is a virtue, but it is not the only one, and I do not think the committee should prefer the more finished candidate to the more consequential one unless the more consequential one is shown to rest on something unsettled. His lineage disclosure to John Hall is a scientific tradition, not a conflict, and I would not ask that it affect his vote, only that it be on the record, as Pearce asks.

responses.point: Eriksson says the omissions in B013 cannot be repaired within a three-name cap and should be stated openly, while keeping Bistritzer because the prediction is joint, and Pearce and Eriksson both treat a two-name MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero version as defensible.
responses.response: I agree with the call for openness and I answer the chair's credit question this way. The rule I would apply is that credit goes to the decisive prediction and to the decisive experimental programme, and within the prediction to the authors of the paper, not to a single senior author. Bistritzer is the first author of the 2011 paper and removing him would split a joint result without a principle. The two-name version is defensible only if the prize is meant to honour theory-and-experiment in outline, and I do not think it is better. Cao and Fatemi cannot be added without exceeding three people, and swapping any one of the three for them would be arbitrary in the other direction. I would therefore keep the three names and ask the committee to record the omissions in its public commentary, which he suggests, and I would not word the citation to claim that the three did all the experimental work.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, has moved from B009 to B061 because the clock has the broadest support, the smallest attribution problem and consequences that are already measured, and he sees B013 as the stated first alternative with readiness the main difference.
responses.response: I take his experimentalist point seriously, that consequences already measured carry more weight than consequences anticipated, and for that reason I regard B061 as my first alternative rather than a distant one. But B013's consequences are also already measured: fractional Chern states, correlated phases in several moire platforms and tunable superconductivity are results, not promises, and the field has changed its experimental practice. On his question about readiness, the pending redefinition of the second is a reason for B061 to be recognised later at no cost, while the moire field's interpretations are moving, so I see both as possibly improved by waiting. That symmetry means the timing argument does not decide between them, and the criterion about the kind of discovery does.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B034 for the cleanest two-name credit and conceptual originality, and says the 2012 prize honoured experimental control of ions and photons and not the theory of using them as gates and simulators.
responses.response: That distinction is fair and is a stronger reading of the 2012 citation than I allowed in round 1, so I now place B034 as a serious alternative. My remaining difficulty is the discovery criterion: the proposals are original, but they are a blueprint whose realisation came largely through experiments that are outside the credited pair, and the citation would need to be drawn narrowly to avoid the ion and cold-atom record already honoured. He himself concedes that B013 and B061 have broader support, and that is a signal but not a reason. I would accept B034 only if the committee decides that a theory-led prize is the right type this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the omission of Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and other experimental and early-theory contributors as acceptable when stated openly in the public commentary, or as a reason to defer B013.
Whether the unresolved superconducting pairing mechanism will change which correlated states prove to be the lasting results, even though the flat-band prediction and the observed phases are secure.
Whether B061 should be preferred because its claim and credit are cleaner; I cannot adjudicate the atomic-physics details myself and rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson for them.

My expertise lies in statistical and complex-systems physics and not in moire quantum materials, atomic clocks or quantum information, so my weighting of the criteria rests on general judgement and on the technical statements of colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round 1 disclosure. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the credited names for B013, B061 or B034 appears among my documented co-authors or supervisors, and my research on turbulent particles, random matrices and complex systems is outside these fields. I treat that as a limit on my expertise, not as a conflict. I note the disclosures of Kroll (lineage to John Hall's laboratory), Johansson (Chalmers and WACQT links, recusal from B018) and Olsson (recusal from B056), and none of them touches my preferred configuration.
